doc.title: John Fedchock interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 28, 2015

chapter: Making a living in New York
title: What jazz students do not learn: people skills
summary: He urges students to be personable with everyone because the business assumes you play well.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: It’s interesting you said that because I wrote down this question I wanted to ask you: what don’t jazz students learn in school?

You know when I go to schools I say, “look around this room. Someone in this room is going to get you a really good gig one day. So it would behoove you all to be very nice to everybody.” Because it may be someone who’s playing third trombone in the third jazz band, and you’re looking down at him like this guy’s nothing. And then later on he’s not playing anymore but he owns a jazz club because he loves jazz. Or he’s an exec on a

record label or something. So all these things come back. And I try to tell students not only the people in this music school, but try to interact with people outside of the music building. Because when you’re talking to like record executives or advertising people when you’re playing a jingle for somebody, you know, they don’t speak the language, the musical language. I mean we get so used to talking to other musicians because it’s comfortable. We can talk about the same kinds of things. But sometimes you have to deal with people that are not musicians and if you can endear yourself to them that’s like gold in the music industry. Executives, and there are some contractors in New York that don’t play, that are not musicians. They wish they could be musicians a lot of them. But they’re not really players. So just having a feeling of being able to interact with people comfortably. Because the last thing you want to do is make someone uncomfortable. If you’re making them uncomfortable they’re not going to want to have you around so you’re not going to get hired. So that’s a lot of what the music business is, because it’s assumed everybody plays well. It’s just assumed. If you’re in New York as a professional musician, you’ve got to be a good player. So that’s just — everyone assumes that. It’s all the other stuff that makes or breaks you.
Oh that’s a great statement. It’s like being in the NBA. There’s no bad basketball players.

And I can imagine learning to like keep inside yourself certain things you want to say. Like if you’re dealing with an ad exec or something that just thinks they know how to talk about music and they say stupid things and you want to like correct them.
Yeah. You can’t overstep that kind of stuff. But yet you need to be personable and make a good impression.
